newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO, envoys weigh response to Mostar report.
newsitem.headline: NATO, envoys weigh response to Mostar report.

text.p: NATO officers and Western envoys on Monday discussed the politically sensitive outcome of an investigation by international police into ethnic violence in the divided Bosnian town of Mostar.

A Moslem man was killed and 22 other Moslems were wounded when armed Croats attacked them when they tried to visit a cemetery on February 10 in the worst violence since peace was signed in December 1995.

The International Police Task Force (IPTF) has not released its findings but NATO officers said photographs showed Croats carrying pistols and batons assaulting the Moslems while Croat police stood by.
NATO officers and deputies to the international High Representative to Bosnia, Carl Bildt, were expected to hold talks with Moslem and Croat leaders on Tuesday.
A spokesman for the Moslem member of the Bosnian collective presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, said he expected the report to blame Croat authorities in western Mostar.
"From the evidence shown, I think it would be difficult to shy away from naming the responsible individuals," spokesman Mirza Hajric told Reuters.
Bosnian Croat police in western Mostar suspended six officers after accusing them of abusing their authority during the incident.
Bildt's office has urged the Croatian government and its Bosnian Croat proteges to halt nationalist "chauvinism" in Mostar.

"The authorities in Zagreb have influence and if they really want, along with other Croat leaders, they can put a stop to this sort of nonsense in Mostar," spokesman Colum Murphy told Bosnian state television in Sarajevo.
The violence in Mostar coincided with a political crisis inside the Moslem-Croat federation and was followed by a wave of expulsions of Moslems from the Croat-controlled western sector.
